ut_seclusion.blurb: Seclusion is a small bouldering spot in Hobble Creek Canyon, east of Springville in the southern Wasatch. The problems sit on a short wall right beside the road, so there is hardly any walk and it suits a quick session. Ten problems run mostly from V0 up to V4, which makes it friendly for newer boulderers while leaving a few harder lines for stronger climbers. Expect short climbs with a corner or two and some stemming, a dark streak of rock in places, and fossils near the top of some lines. Loose rocks can sit on top, so top out with care and bring a crash pad.

ut_gin_tectonics.blurb: Gin & Tectonics is a sunny, south-facing sandstone wall in Long Canyon, a short drive from Moab off the Potash Road. It is a trad crag with ten routes, all between 5.10 and 5.12, so it is aimed at strong climbers rather than beginners. The wall is known for splitter cracks, including an obvious offwidth, and several lines run to multiple pitches. Because the wall gets plenty of sun, the cooler months are the comfortable time to visit. The rock is sandstone, so loose pieces can turn up on lesser-travelled lines, and you will want a full trad rack.

ut_g_crags.blurb: G Crags is a group of east-facing sandstone slabs in the Eastern Reef, nicknamed the Sandstone Alps, in the San Rafael Swell of central Utah. The ten routes are all trad and mostly moderate: a few at 5.6, a cluster in the 5.8 to 5.9 range, and one 5.10a. The reef as a whole is a huge slab formation where the rock is generally good but has the odd soft spot, and pitches can be long and sparsely protected, so it rewards climbers who are comfortable on slab. Camping near the head of the nearby canyon makes it practical to spend a weekend out here.

ut_k_crags.blurb: K Crags is a slab-climbing sector of the Eastern Reef, also known as the Sandstone Alps, in the San Rafael Swell of south-central Utah. It holds ten trad routes between 5.6 and 5.9, which makes it one of the gentler corners of a reef better known for big, committing lines. The slabs are praised as some of the best you will find, but several routes carry an R rating and can be runout in places, so solid footwork and a calm head matter more than strength. The rock is sandstone, and the walk in is long, around 40 minutes each way.

ut_upper_division_wall.blurb: Upper Division Wall is a steep, shaded limestone wall in American Fork Canyon in the southern Wasatch, about ten minutes uphill from the more popular Division Wall. It is a hard sport venue: nine bolted routes, all in the 5.12 range with at least one at each letter grade, plus a single V5 boulder problem. The lines start close together, often out of a small cave, and the climbing is steep and pocketed. The wall hangs directly above the lower crag and its parking area, so rockfall is a real concern for people below and kicking down loose rock should be avoided.

ut_intensive_care_slab.blurb: Intensive Care Slab is a south-facing slab perched high in a gully between Church Buttress and The Fin in Little Cottonwood Canyon. It holds ten routes, mostly trad with a couple of bolted lines, spread from 5.7 up through the 5.10s and into 5.11. Expect delicate face climbing with sustained slab moves and the occasional crack, and some of the harder routes are serious, with sparse protection. It is well worth the trip on its own, or as a few extra routes after rappelling off The Fin.

ut_prune_face_slab.blurb: Prune Face Slab is a roughly 100-foot, moderately featured slab on the Gate Buttress in Little Cottonwood Canyon, just downslope from the Five Fingers area. Its short approach, only a few minutes, is the quickest on the buttress. Ten routes, nearly all trad plus one bolted line, run from 5.7 through the 5.10s with a single 5.11. The climbing is mostly classic slab with some grooves, the easier lines feel sustained, and a few routes are runout. Moves can be thin low down on the harder lines, and the top anchors are set up for lowering off.

ut_convent_the_2.blurb: The Convent is a small sandstone bouldering area inside Pioneer Park on the north side of St. George. Ten problems range from V1 to V5, with most falling in the V2 to V3 band, so it suits climbers working through the moderate grades. The rock is solid low down but softer on the top-outs, which can feel unsettling if you are new to the desert. It holds a bit more shade than the rest of the park, a useful bonus in hot weather. The park is busy with visitors and families, and broken glass has been a nuisance, so watch your step around the cave.
